My personal chronology with the "Princess Leia" hologram.

The movie came out in summer of 1977 I am pretty sure, as I was bonding with my junior high math classes with it. (Me being the teacher, of course!) If it wasn't 1977, then it must have been '78. And I remember in the first cut in the theatres, the "projected" Leia looking snowy staticy, with rainbow banding. Just thought of it as an artifact of whatever futuristic device that the special effects were trying to simulate.

Then I first saw a Multiplex hologram in Fall of 1978, and that was when I realized what they were trying to emulate in SW! Of course, embossed was just a gleam in Steve McGrew and Ken Haines and a few others' eyes at that time, and the general public probably was just as clueless as I was about the "holographic" rendering in the movie. Unless of course if you lived in SF or other places where holos were exhibited back then.

If you check out more current reissues of the SW #4, I think they took out the Multiplex rainbow artifact.

So I am not too sure about Liti's claim that the Leia projection fired up the public's imagination! (Along with a bunch of their other claims!)

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
I also think it depends on what you mean by "projection". If you take the classical idea of a projection as the magnification and focusing of an amplitude modulated surface onto a larger surface, such as a slide projected on a screen, then this is simply the recreation of a particular amplitude modulation and clearly a hologrm is not a projection and neither is a rainbow. If you take any wavefront, magnify it and focus it at another pojnt in space, such as the curved mirror images of eg the Haunted House ghosts, then again neither a hologram or a rainbow are projections. In the curved mirror case, the original wavefront of an object is copied and displaced on a larger scale by means of the mirror. The wavefront being produced by a hologram is generated by diffraction off a fringe structure and is not a copy or a displacement of an existing wavefront. The rainbow is caused by collimated sunlight through reflections and refractions - again, not a copy of an existing wavefront. In both hologram and rainbow, a new wavefront is created from another, different wavefront. If the existence of any image in space is considered as a projection, then reality itself must be seen as a projection, since any tactile sense is independant of visual stimulation. A hologram of a cat is just as much a projection as is a real cat which you cannot touch, especially since no visual test can distinguish between a hologram of a cat and a real cat from any given viewpoint. They're the same wavefront!

In the example of the H2, the H2 captures an interference pattern arising from the wavefront of the H1 and the wavefront of the reference. Both wavefronts are necessary, and yet the reference beam is not thought of as a projection. In my view, the H2 is the result of two wavefronts, either of which can be independantly created. So, if you had a small box with fine droplets of suspended water, shone collimated white light through it, placed a plate at an appropriiate distance and zapped it with a reference, you'd get a hologram of a rainbow. Recording it may be tough, since you'd need truly panchromatic film! A little more simple - have two H1's on either side of a plate. Have the H1 image of one reference the H1 image of the other. Let's say an H1 with a cat and an H1 of a model of the Enterprise (The old one, I'm a fan of the old one!). Now, if the resulting H2 is placed in front of the real Enterprise, brightly lit, then the hologram of the cat shows up. Which is now the projection?

[quote:4a5ba35eb3="edelbrp"]What if you took a standard water/rain shower and shined something other than collimated white light at it? Could you produce a holographic effect if you specially craft light of different colors pointed in different directions (and source locations)? That could be interesting. [/quote:4a5ba35eb3]

Actually, this is what the computer-generated holograpy people do. Basically, you're generating a new waveform from a set of different waveforms of different directions and phases. The computer calculates the different directions and phases of a waveform, you're generating these by placing appropriate water droplets of different sizes (phase variations) and causing different directions by refractions of light from varying directions.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
My, my, my, I'm off-line for a couple of days and things get very interesting! Latest topics in this thread first!

Rant Phase 1: A rainbow has nothing to do with diffraction, projection, or wavefront reconstruction. When you're looking at a rainbow you are looking at the dispersed output of tons of spherical "prisms". (Prisms are in quotes because a sphere could not be a prism in the sense of the mathematical definition of "a solid having regular polygons for the bases and rectangles for its sides." But a sphere can be a dispersing element like the ever popular equilateral triangle prism. Read on.)

Think of the circumstance of when you see a rainbow. The sun is directly behind you and you are looking into the distance, your eyes pointing in the direction of your attached shadow, at a curtain of raindrops.

The sunlight coming from behind you passes you by, and enters the drops in front of you. The paraxial rays (through the dead nuts center and a bit further out) pass through the drop, and come to a focus very close to the outside surface of the water globule. After the focus, the cone of light expands quite rapidly, going off in many other directions other than parallel to the original incident ray. To an observer on the opposite side of the rain curtain compared our position the sunlight is attenuated, a dark curtain, not totally because of reflectivity and density but of a change in direction due to refraction.

Rays of light incident on the whole convex hemisphere of the drop that is looking at the sunlight are refracted inward as they enter the dihydrous oxide. We saw what happens to the central rays above, but after a certain distance from the center (the actual distance is left as an exercise to the reader!) the rays cannot escape the drop because their angle of incidence is >= the critical angle. The are Totally Internally Reflected.

The rays at the top of the drop are reflected downward by the concave surface they are now encountering on their exit path. But they are not reflected anti-parallel to their original angle of incidence since we are not dealing with a corner cube.

In the case of the rays of light that entered the very tippy-top of the drop these rays are reflected straight down to earth with an angle between 40 and 42 degrees compared to the original incident sunlight.

To find the angle with precision, the wavelength needs to be specified, as the white sunlight disperses at the first surface entrance refraction and a bit more at the second surface exit refraction. The red angle is not the same as the blue angle. (Again, the reader could work out the table of angles versus wavelengths, but better still look at one fo the popular books on optics, such as **Seeing the Light**, Falk, Brill & Stork, p.65; **Light Science**, Rossing & Chiaverena, p.3; **The Universe of Light**, Bragg, p.110. The scenario created above is related to the ray traces above by looking at the illustrations not dead on by in the plane of the edge of the paper! {Looking at the page's edge} [Somebody should illustrate optics books with holograms of these 3-D vectors!]

If the angles were computed, it would be found that the even further from the center, the edge rays would eventually no longer refract out of the drop but bango! get TIR'ed again back into the drop! Now this time they are heading skyward plus or minus 51 degrees relative to the incident sunlight, in addition to getting dispersed twice, but this spectrum is heading skyward, so only planes could see this rainbow!

But we haven't discussed the edge rays that entered on the earthward side of the drop. In this area, the rays that are singly TIR'ed head heavenward, and the double reflections head down to the devil, or us if we are so lucky, and this is the origin of the secondary rainbow. But this is a rare occasion, and very hard to photograph.

And rays even further to the edge would be triply TIR'ed, and end up who knows where but I did see in an Amateur Scientist in Scientific American that there theoretically could be 21 different rainbows! (A calculation best left to Dinesh!)

This dispersion that ends up in our eyes is from rays entering along a diameter that is perfectly vertical. Rays that are entering the edge that are at say, one o'clock compared to the vertical will not only do the dance above but come out at a skew, anti-altazimuthal to be sure, i.e., the one o'clock comes out at seven direction.

The top of the 'bow is directly in front of us. When your eye shifts to the right, the ray that will enter it will not come from the same level in the curtain of raindrops as the one that is at the top of the drop but from one lower. (To help imagine this in 3-D, look at the thin edge of one of the above optics books along the line of the downward heading first rainbow ray. Then shift your gaze, and you should be able to envision approximately where the dispersed and TIR'ed and skewed ray should be coming from.)

I saw in a comic book in my youth a *Science Fact* that a viewer in an airplane should be able to see a completely circular rainbow rainbow! Consider the above and you should be able to see how this could be true! But I haven't seen any photos (but I haven't looked hard!)

There exists a corresponding physical (wave-like) optical explanation.

I'm sorry for this verbal diarrhea but I am a college professor having been teaching this lesson about seven times a year for the past 20 years.

Rant Phase 2:

No, I don't think the average Joe would have ever connected Princess Leia in the original screenings with holography. I have always thought of myself as being fairly literate image-wise, having printed B & W and color photos since high school, going to museums and galleries, teaching night school photography to suburbanites who bought the latest tech status symbol of that era, the 35 mm SLR, (basically explaining to them what each button did), attending Chicago Stereo Camera Club meetings, but it wasn't until I went to the fall 1978 Society of Photographic Education Midwest Convention that I saw holograms up close and personal thanks to TJ, who was giving a talk and for a fee you could see him do his magic show!

He had a 360 Multiplex of his kids doing "Hear no Evil, See no Evil, Speak No Evil". He made a Single Beam Reflection and a Single Beam Transmission of junk from his pocket so no one would complain that he had the props prepared. He had Russian holograms, one of which was a stereogram, the holographer with his car, but I don't recall any rainbow holos. And I got hooked. 

(Coincidentally, DEVO appeared on Saturday Night Live that night. Everyone else in the room looking at the tube looked like they had big question marks hanging over their heads like in the funny papers. I was in heaven. The day that changed my life.)

For sure the first rainbow holograms that I candefinitely recall seeing were at Gallery 1134 (some of you know them by the Chicago Museum of Holography, but I call them by the number of their beast, as you will realize by looking at the above digits upside down on your pocket calculator.) when I made my first visit there. The one that stands out the most vivid is the classic Lon Moore Desert Scene.

The first embossed holos I saw were when I worked at the above. They were from Steve McGrew's new Light Impressions. There was a bird skull on a rock and a heart with a rock, both images attributed to John Kaufman, and a masked off graphics grating sunrise or sunset, I don't know which, something like what would be called a 2D/3D or "a dropped in image" nowadays. I remember John Hoffmann, who still works there, criticizing them, telling Loren Billings how much sharper and brighter he could make them. And she was so much in love with him that she believed him! (Steve Provence takes credit as being the beam jockey for the originations.)

This could have been no later than June of 1981, as that is when I escaped from there with my life! No kidding, 3 or 4 people that I knew from there died in a year! But that's a spooky story for a campfire and a keg.

But I took a motorcycle trip south and then east, arriving in NY and working at the real **Museum of Holography**for a week. There I saw some sort of replicated hologram by Mike Foster, I can't recall if it was a Benton type, but it was definitely transmission, not metallic backed. I think it was like an aquatic scene. Hopefully this thing still exists in some form in Cambridge. And documentation.

Yeah, who knows who really did what in the field of embossed holography. It seems to me that it all kind of stems from the RCA SelectaVision project, a holographic video storage device that would be in everyone's home in the 21st Century, except for one little thing: the videocassette. Viz. the seminal photo-resist paper of Bartolini. (I'm too pooped to find this and other citations!)

I didn't cite Holovision as I don't personally have one in my personal museum, much less ever seen their wares. I might have an article on them in my library that I compiled by going through the **Reader's Guide to Periodical Literature**(the Google of the '70's, god how I'm dating myself!) and Xeroxing every one thanks to the holdings at the University of Illinois, Urbana, plus Sixties and Seventies issues of Laser Focus (before that added World) and Optical Spectra (before they changed to Photonics Spectra) that I rescued when TJ was going to throw them out. It would be super holo-history scholarship to find out more.

Interestingly enough, both of these mag's of that era had at least one article or blurb about holography in each issue unlike today. A lot of the articles were probably just as disturbing to the holographers in the trenches of yore as the Liti's of today! If you have plenty of time on your hands and plenty of copy machine coins you should try to find '60's and '70's Pop Science and Pop Mechanics (there were two back then!) or similar, at your local library, (like as if they preserved them. But isn't that what they're supposed to be doing?) For sure I know Life or Look, back when they were big, and I mean in size not necessarily circulation, had an article with a beautiful picture of an S-P 185 He-Cd in the Selectavision recording setup. If you do the research you will be splendidly rewarded.

I conjecture that people from Lucas Films had seen Multiplexes prior to the filming of SW, as they were a San Fran Company and would have had a presence on the West Coast in the mid-70's. Someone involved with them would know better than me. And that was their inspiration for the way they simulated the holographic projection, with scores of articles in the magazines mentioned above shilling the possibility. Only if you lived in a place where someone put on a holography show would you have seen one.

While doing the research above it appears that Edmund Scientific was selling laser transmission holograms based on ad's found in Scientific American, in issues that I would have read in high school, but it didn't have any effect on me, only until I saw one in person did it click.

Well, I guess this answers the question of what a lonely old holographer does on a Saturday night!

Yes, true. My point was that any optical effect that created an image "floating" in space seems to be thought of as a "projection". Well, a rainbow certainly fits that description and so, by rights, it should also be called a "projection", but never is. And yet there are numerous people who call a hologram, or rather a holographic image, a projection. The funny thing is, an image-planed hologram is not a projection, but an image a distance away from the plate, eg an H1, is. Certainly a flat object image planed right on the plate would never be considered a projection.

I suppose my rant is that I've never thought of a hologram as a projection. To me, a projection is the translation and (maybe) a magnification of an image wherein the existing waveform is simply copied. Both a hologram and a rainbow are waveforms created from other waveforms in situ. There's probably a more elegant way of saying this that escapes me for now, but if a waveform were to be converted into another waveform which would then create an image in "free space", then sunlight coming in from your window, hitting your sofa and creating a waveform of a sofa by reflections and diffractions and causing an image of a sofa apparently hanging in free space implies that your sofa is a projection (so long as you don't touch it).

I suppose it's minor, and probably a bit pedantic. However, by thinking of a hologram as some sort of projection, it's then very easy to believe in a Princess Leia (why are those words never acronym-ised? Star Wars becomes SW, but Princess Leia never becomes PL ). Once this concept takes hold, it's very difficult to dislodge it. part of the mystique, and later disappointment, of the public at large is that this concept of "projection" is so often associated with a holographic image. I was recently asked if I could reproduce the "hologram" in the film "Ocean's Twelve"!

Thanks, Ed, for that lucid explanation of rainbows. It's actually quite a difficult problem. It was first cracked by Airy in the mid-19th century and finally completed by Lord Rayleigh towards the end of the century. The exterior angle of the refraction, as shown by Edelbrp, is 42 degrees. When Joy discovered this, she thought she had The Answer to Life, The Universe and Everything a la Hitchhiker's Guide ("What is 42?"). She mentioned this to the teacher of an SF class she took who happened to know Douglas Adams. The teacher said he'd never thought of it, but Douglas Adams himself probably had that in mind!

I can confirm that the rainbow is an entire circle. I've seen it from an airplane window. I started drawing one inch lines using the upper joint of my thumb as approx one inch to create a grid on paper. I then placed the paper against the window and tried to see what the diameter was, and if it became larger or smaller as the plane descended. Luckily the plane was descending at the time. Knowing that commercial jetliners cruise at approx 35,000 feet and knowing how long it would take to get down to sea level, I had the rate of descent, dh/dt. By taking succesive measurements of the diameter, D, of the rainbow I could get dD/dt. It was now simple to get the rate of change of diameter of circular rainbow to height, dD/dh, if any. Unfortunately the hostess started giving me funny looks and asked me, very pointedly, to sit back! I half thought to see if I could calculate this theoretically, but never got around to it.

In this case, I think Kaveh was bemaoning the fact that Liti were implying that the PL image was "projected hologram". Certainly I'd think that the average public would infer from this that PL ( Good god! Youve got me acronymising now ) was a)a hologram and b)was projected.

I take that to mean that John thinks of the H1 pseudo image as "a projection" as opposed to the actual fringe structure being projected. So, I'd say that it seems that a holographic image apparently flaoting in free space, as for instance the pseudo image from a H1 or a white light image image-planed a long way off the plate, is seen as a "projection". However, in both these cases, the image is seen as free floating. A standard, relatively shallow, white light reflection is not see as a "projection" because it doesn't seem to freely float. However, in both these cases (free floating images off the image plane and image-planed white light reflection) the image is holographically generated, ie diffracted from a series of fringes created interferometrically. They're both "whole images" - actually a misnomer if applied to the image since I believe the "whole" part referred to the fact that the entire image data was smeared over the entire plate so that every part of the plate contained the "whole image". It's the plate that's "the whole image", not the image itself. I think of a projection as not a newly generated waveform due to diffraction or refraction, but an existing waveform that's been displaced. So an object strongly illuminated and placed at a certain position on the axis of a curved mirror would create an image of that object at another part of the axis of the mirror. It's still a 3D ("whole image"?) image and you can almost walk around it, but it's not generated by diffraction. The waveform is not created from fringes, but is a displaced copy of the original object waveform.

[quote:44013dc2a8="MichaelH"]On the other hand, why wouldn't a projection of the PL type be a hologram? The term roughly translates into "whole image" and if a PL projection can be walked around so that you can see her from all sides (something you can't do with most contemporary holograms) will it not be a "hologram"?[/quote:44013dc2a8]

Because a hologram is either the image generated by diffraction from a set of interferometrically-created fringes, or is the actual fringe structure from which an image may, or may not (HOE's) be generated. If the "whole image" part is translated as being the capability to view an image that's representative of an object in it's entirety, then I'd say that Greg Favalora's system ( [http://www.actuality-systems.com/index. ... y/products](http://www.actuality-systems.com/index.php/actuality/products) ) is more of a hologram than anything we "holographers" can make, because his system does indeed give you a full 360 degree view and the image represents all the data of the object at any view and perspective. However, Gregg's system is based of computer graphics techniques, not diffraction. So the question becomes: "Is Holography defined by the image, or by the technique of recording fringes" If by the image, where would you place acoustic holography? Can the image of an acoustic hologram recorded on water be projected?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: As I said, light itself is invisible. You can't see light. You need matter in order to make light visible. If you consider a hologram as a series of lenses embedded into the emulsion of different focal lengths, then a reconstruction beam essentially is a beam that hits these lenses and is focused by them to different parts of space. Like any real lenses, the focal point depends on the origin point of the light, if the light comes from infinity, ie it's collimated, then the light will focus at the focal length of the lens. If not, the light will focus somewhere beyond the focal length. Now you have this multiple set of focused points of light. At these points, if matter is present, such as a fog of particles from a mist, then this matter interacts with the light and sends it out as a spherical, outward wave. The sum of all the focused points of light will create an image, provided the fog is extensive enough and lasts long enough. However, if there's no matter there, the light will simply diverge from the focused point. With nothing there to scatter it, whatever image data it contains will not be seen. If you changed the index at the focal point by, eg, creating a "hot spot", then the light at the focal point will change it's velocity, since the velocity of light depends on the index, but will still be invisible. You need some form of matter to scatter the light. It's vaguely possible to view the collection of points, and hence the image, by observing the area of focus with an IR camera if you can get the temperature differential high enough and/or your IR camera was sensitive enough. It's also possible that if the index change were high enough (and local enough) you'd get reflection due to the interface between two indices, but the index change needs to be very rapid. If the index change occurs within roughly lambda/2, the Fresnel equations will apply and the index interface will scatter. But you're talking a significant change in temperature within roughly 250nm for a spot that itself is about a micron or two across. I doubt it'd be stable for very long.

Not quite. When light propagates through a medium, let's say a slab of glass, the molecules of the glass are intersperced at roughly the same distance. As the light propagates, each molecule vibrates due to incoming light and creates light in all directions. Only the forward proagations actually "go through", not the side and backwards propagations. Hence a beam of light in the glass does not go to the sides or the back, only forward. Now if you slice the glass at some intermediate point, you have back reflection where none existed before. This is because there is an "abrupt" change in molecular density. The backwards propagating light from the sliced interface of the glass meets a "new set" of molecules (air molecules) which is not as dense as the ones in the glass. Hence this new set of molecules can no longer destructivly interfere with the backwards propagating light from the interior molecules of the glass and the backward propagating light comes into existence. However, this change must exist fairly quickly. If the change in molecular density is slow, the change in density is slow and will not create a backward propagation. Depending on the exact nature of the rate of falling off of molecular distances, the backwards beam will simply slowly die off over a few molecular diameters. Same with a "hot air bubble. The heat creates a different molecular density. hence the distinction between the molecular density of the "hot spot" must be distinct and quick. If the heat gradually cools down over a few molecular distances, the density difference is too slow and the back propagation will not be strong.

The shimmering image on the road is not caused by reflections, but by refractions. Hot air has a lower density, and hence a lower refractive index. What you have is not an abrupt reflective surface, but a startified medium of slow index change. As the heat shimmers, the reflected light from the road surface takes different paths, trying to find the "path of minimum time" through media in which it's velocity is constantly changing over small distances. You'll also notice that you don't get that same shimmering on a cloudy day. No reflection off the road surface, except when car headlights reflect off it over a bump in the road. Imagine water going through a sponge. A uniform sponge will allow uniform flow. However, if you have a "Maxwells demon" constantly and sporadically changing the local density of the sponge, the path of the water will be erratic as it wanders through the sponge. 

Your "hot spot" will effectively behave the same. Unless it's very hot and highly localised, some of the incoming light will refract away from the direct path, but only by a few degrees.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
I think this ended up in the wrong place....

By the way, only the press think Benton invented the embossing technique. He "invented" the techniqure of viewing display HIGS in white light by restricting the aperture. and so the dispersion. The so-called "Rainbow". 

The fact that this is the main vehicle for embossed holography came from the fact that the spatial frequencies of these HIGS are low enough to capture image data as a surface profile. The average spatial frequency of a rainbow HIG is approx 1000 l/mm which is achievable in materials such as photoresist and thermoplastics (the frequency response of photoresists ca 1977 was approx 1500 l/mm with the response function falling exponentially at around 1200 l/mm). The average spatial frequency of a reflection HIG is about 3000 l/mm - too high for resists of the period and even now. Of course, once the image data can be captured as a surface profile, it was possible by electroforming to copy this data and so mass produce it.

I understand Steve himself wasn't too happy about embossed. Jonathan Ross tells of an account of a visit to Steve at Polaroid. The story is in the commemorative issue of SPIE Technical Group Newsletter, vol 15, no 1. In it he's none too exuberant about ebossed holograms. I won't quote it, since it's..well..perhaps a little risque. If you have a copy of this magazine, you'll find the quote on p.11 .

I didn't think anyone believed Stephen invented 'embossed' holography, in fact if we must be purely essential about this... it was RCA's HoloTape that came first. 

> I understand Steve himself wasn't too happy about embossed. Jonathan Ross tells of an account of a visit to Steve at Polaroid. The story is in the commemorative issue of SPIE Technical Group Newsletter, vol 15, no 1. In it he's none too exuberant about ebossed holograms. I won't quote it, since it's..well..perhaps a little risque. If you have a copy of this magazine, you'll find the quote on p.11 .

I've heard Steve's views about embossed holography, from Steve... they mirror mine... but that night in 1977 when I succeeded in converting a Cross Multiplex of the Death Star blowing up into 50 embossed copies... I nonetheless felt real! good. Previous to that moment, Benton Rainbows had never been mass produced via embossing (well at least in this country, maybe in Japan). That year we turned out many thousands of embossments, I thought it was all good... so damn good! Who would have known that I couldn't even give embossed holograms away at the shopping center as samples! There was still enough market to sell thousands all over the world, but to approach someone and try and give them one.... meant nothing... kids loved the colors, adults thought they were 'neat', but no one seemed to want to keep them. I knew then that there was money to make in embossments, but the idea of making millions of dollars on them, .... no way. On the other hand ..... Dichromates, it was obvious, they were a different story.
